Subscribe --> Donate Log In By Eric Olander A truck drives along a road past the Port of Ngqura in the Coega Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Nelson Mandela Bay on September 29, 2026. The zone hosts companies across sectors including automotive manufacturing, logistics, agro-processing and energy. (Photo by EMMANUEL CROSET / AFP) South Africa’s exclusion from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) marks a turning point in its economic relationship with the United States, putting an estimated 100,000 jobs and $1.7 billion in exports at risk. As trade tensions deepen, Pretoria is accelerating efforts to diversify its economic partnerships, with China increasingly central to that shift.
But replacing one trading partner with another carries its own risks. Persistent trade imbalances, dependence on mineral exports and limited access to high-value markets raise questions about the benefits of deeper economic ties with China. Meanwhile, proposals to connect the Benguela and TAZARA railways point to a broader ambition to strengthen African trade and continental integration.
Cobus, Geraud and Eric discuss South Africa’s changing trade relationships, China’s expanding manufacturing footprint in Africa, and the future of regional infrastructure and intra-African trade.
ERIC OLANDER: Hello and welcome to another edition of the China in Africa podcast, a proud member of the Sinica podcast network. I’m Eric Olander. Today, I’m coming to you from the Nairobi podcast studio in central Nairobi, thrilled to be in Kenya.
We’re here for a week, talking with a whole bunch of people and working with journalists here. So we’re going to tell you a little bit more about what we’re doing, but as always, I’m joined not from Mauritius or from South Africa normally, but here with me in the studio, Geraud Neema, our Africa editor, and Cobus van Staden, our head of research. Gentlemen, great to see you in Nairobi.
ERIC OLANDER: And back in a podcast studio. Only when we come to Africa do we get these great podcast studios.
So today, listen, we’re going to talk about a couple of different things. One, we’re going to focus on the thing that everybody’s talking about. This is the AGOA, which is South Africa.
And the way that they were framing it in South Africa was that South Africa has graduated out of AGOA. That is French for South Africa got booted out of AGOA by the Trump administration. And then we’re also going to talk about what that kind of speaks to in terms of the larger vision that the U.S. and other powers, including China, have for China. OK, so, Cobus, this is in your neighborhood. The United States made it clear today we had suspected this was going to be the case that they, Rwanda and South Africa, Rwanda, this is the second time now that it’s been booted out of AGOA. They are no longer welcome into the African Growth and Opportunity Act for tariff-free entry into the United States.
Let’s remember this was not tariff-free. This was Liberation Day tariff. Tell us more about how this was received in South Africa.
COBUS VAN STADEN: You know, South Africa had been preparing for this for a while, so it wasn’t 100 percent news, but it still is very dismaying, I think, for them. There’s about 100,000 jobs on the line.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Yes. And I think, you know, on the AGOA side, South Africa’s trade made up more than half of AGOA trade. So this really takes down AGOA as a trade measure.
But on the South African side, the South African government put a kind of happy spin on it by emphasizing how hard they’ve been working to diversify their partners. So into Africa, into Asia, into Europe, and Asia being particularly into China. So, you know, and so, yeah, you know, so South Africans, I think, have expected it.
But still, it’s bad for South Africa. You know, it’s particularly for the automotive industry.
ERIC OLANDER: There was a lot of showboating on X and social media saying, you know, F them, we don’t need them. I think that’s, if your job isn’t tied to AGOA, that’s pretty easy to say. But there are 100,000 jobs in a country that has 47, 48 percent unemployment.
This comes at a tough time for South Africa. Definitely, it comes at a very tough time for South Africa.
GERAUD NEEMA: For me, when I look at it, I think, anyways, Sri Ramaphosa, the South African President, has said that already. They were ready that they were going to be booted out of AGOA. I think they reached a point of, like, we’ve tried everything.
We accepted the humiliation. We accepted getting a very racist ambassador to our country. We agreed to even send another ambassador to the United States to try to appease the Trump administration.
But obviously, everything that we’ve tried doesn’t work, did not work. I remember the South African ambassador saying that we don’t know what they want. We put a proposal on the table.
They just say, “No”, without a counterproposal. What was the issue? So this is where the AGOA booting and South Africa being booted out of AGOA, it’s become much more about geopolitics than anything else, because you look at the reason why you don’t have a clear understanding, like, why are you booting South Africa out of AGOA? And RUN is a different story.
RUN is about the US and DRC and Eastern DRC and all of that. But South Africa is like, we don’t understand it. I think now, for South Africa, the challenge is: how do you replace that?
What’s the alternative? It’s true that we’re talking about looking east, finding opportunities. We’re also looking into when you talk about that, we have a big part of being U.S. and European investment in the automotive industry. We’re seeing Chinese companies moving into South Africa for that. So are we going to see a shift of Chinese also kind of making it up for that gap that’s going to be left out of the industry, or South Africa is going to have to find itself a way out of that?
ERIC OLANDER: Part of the dismay that the South African delegation mentioned was something that the Canadians also talked about in their negotiations with the Trump administration over trade was that, at the last minute, the Americans started inserting all these different things that they hadn’t been prepared for. And it took them by surprise. They couldn’t reach a negotiation.
So everything kind of fell apart. Now, let’s talk about this pivot to the east. On the day that the AGOA news broke, the Chinese ambassador to South Africa, Wu Peng, who’s been on our show before, posted a tweet.
And again, what we have now is an ex post. Let me just read it. And he’s really said growing China-South Africa trade tells a story of win-win cooperation.
We’ve heard that rhetoric before. Trade between China and South Africa reached nearly fifteen billion dollars from May to August twenty-six, an increase of twenty-four percent year on year. Over that period, South African exports to China grew by twenty-five percent.
Agricultural exports to China reached four hundred ninety-five million dollars, an increase of more than thirty-five percent. Now, right under that tweet, some guy named Kokaya says he did a funny post, and I’d like to get your take on this. He said Wu Peng is such a certified troll.
Happy smiley face emoji. Whenever Trump hates on South Africa, Wu Peng never fails to enter the chat, dropping the receipts on how well China and South Africa are getting along. So, again, Wu Peng was having a moment saying, listen, if the Americans are going to drop you here, our relationship with you is doing quite well, in fact, growing.
This isn’t necessarily a good thing in one sense, because of the concern that you’ve raised previously about countries being overly dependent on one or two large trading partners. So it’s good to help offset some of the American losses. But long term, it may not be good to become too dependent on one or two countries like the DRC in mining.
Right. I mean, this is not specific to China. It could be any country.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Well, the South Africans have been really kind of reaching out to everyone. Right. And so the kind of trade deals with China is coming on the back of trade deals with Southeast Asia, with the Middle East, and so on.
So in that sense, they, you know, in that sense, a goer could be a kind of cautionary tale about overdependence on one trade partner, you know. And I think South Africa is learning that exactly. Even if President Ossoff is in twenty-nine, South Africa is never going to trust the U.S. again on, you know, kind of in this kind of way. So, you know, they may trade with them again, but they will always keep a kind of a hedge in there.
ERIC OLANDER: But let’s be clear, the critical minerals that the United States depends on South Africa for are exempted from this. Is that your understanding?
ERIC OLANDER: Right. So it’s basically, the deal is the stuff that the Americans don’t really want. They put it they’ve said now you can pay a tariff.
And we’ve been reminded by South Africans that just because a goer is gone doesn’t mean South African trade with the United States goes away.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Yeah, just now trades at a higher tariff. And of course, you know, the people like the people who are tariffed, among others, are American companies, right? Because Ford Motor Company, you know, is one of the main victims of this whole saga.
So, you know, so, you know, yeah, I think. But I think in a larger sense, I think South Africa is like. South Africa is increasingly, I think, has decided, you know, that’s the and we’ll we’ll see how it plays out.
But, you know, but I think that there’s a there’s a growing consensus that South Africa’s economic future lies eastwards, you know, and that and that there is, you know, there may be other relationships to the West, but those aren’t going to be economically transformative. And so in that sense, I think that’s a very fundamental shift, because, you know, because South Africa has been historically very, very close to Western power, very close to Europe, very close to the US. And that has in like within the last less than 10 years, there’s been noticeable shift.
And I don’t think it’s shifting back. Like, you know, who knows? Let’s see.
But, you know, but I think that kind of push away from the US, I think, may be a permanent situation.
GERAUD NEEMA: Definitely. That’s something I think South Africa will have to be innovative about on how to offset that situation. Talking about investment, it’s basically European investments of Africa that’s also going to be hurt.
The Stellantis of this worldwide investment billions of dollars in South Africa in terms of car that was shipping to the US. Now South Africa has to find new markets. But interestingly enough, Europeans that invest in South Africa are not always opening their markets to South African products that are invested in South Africa.
That’s something for me that’s really disturbing. And I think South Africa now, even though we’re talking about East, and I think that’s where Wu Pang was kind of piggybacking on the fact that, yes, you know, our relationship with South Africa is good. I’m going to just point out to a reference why he did mention from May to October, for people who don’t know, May, because since the May 1 tariff, the full, the full, the zero tariffs for Africa.
ERIC OLANDER: 53 African countries are tariff-free exporters to China.
GERAUD NEEMA: Exactly. That’s why he referenced that kind of signaling that us, where others are lifting barriers, we are putting them down. And this is the effect of putting down barriers.
The reality is if you really dig deep in the numbers, you’re like, nah, that’s not really the case. Because when you break down South Africa’s exports to China, it’s like, yes, you have now more fruit, you have stone fruit, you have agricultural product, but you still have heavy, heavy, heavy, heavy export on critical minerals, not critical minerals, minerals as a whole. Mining product, chromium, gold, PGM.
You have that to be the bulk of it. And I know he really made it really fun to say, you know, only 20 billions of minerals. My friend, it’s more than that.
And this is the interesting part of like, yes, it shows a lot because it’s not the first time. It’s really something he does on a regular basis. Every time there is a kind of rift between South Africa and U.S., you know, he kind of drops everything about China. But at the end, China and South Africa will have to resolve two things. First thing, they have to kind of come to agreement about the trade numbers. We know I’ve covered that many times, that China and South Africa have two different trade numbers about the reality.
The numbers that he mentioned is from China Customs. You go to South Africa and revenue services, they’re going to tell you it’s a different numbers and South Africa is running a trade deficit. In China, it’s different.
Second of all, now it’s going to be about the quality of the trade they’re making now. Now, the question becomes, OK, how much the May 1st policy are going to really shift and change South Africa, China trade in a way that even though AGOA is gone, South Africa is still going to have an opportunity to to export to China. But for me, beyond these two countries, South Africa, the U.S., the future and not only for South Africa, the future of many African countries in terms of trade would come inside Africa.
GERAUD NEEMA: And I think this is the gap that we don’t always talk about the fact that we don’t trade a lot among ourselves to be able to offset this kind of issues when they come about AGOA.
COBUS VAN STADEN: And South Africa is a leader on that. And they’ve really been emphasizing that now with this with AGOA thing. And interestingly, the BAIC, the Chinese carmaker now is now like putting out all of these massive billboards all over Johannesburg saying, you know, we manufacture in South Africa.
So this is very interesting. You know, but I think a lot of that manufacturing in South Africa will then go to the African market.
GERAUD NEEMA: They have to. Now the element of ACFTA becoming something. And I think a country like big countries like South Africa and Nigeria should be the one really pushing for the ACFTA as a solution for any kind of radar taking place against them.
But I don’t see that happening yet. And I think this is one of the big challenges we have to address to be able to not be dependent on a single partner. Because let’s not forget, the African market is not one.
It’s not it’s not one partners. It’s 53 different economic partners. So if you open your market to that, if you really have that trade taking place, you don’t really worry about AGOA and everything, but don’t have the issue about Africa will be purchasing power.
Let’s face it, African countries are not rich enough to be buying new cars in the same path.
ERIC OLANDER: Well, yes, but this is where China, to its credit, has done incredibly well. They operate in 2 percent, 3 percent profit margin environments very well. This is where U.S., European, Japanese, Korean companies have said the profits aren’t big enough in Africa, but Chinese companies have moved in. We just saw the secondary offering for Transcend on the Hong Kong exchange. They raised four hundred million dollars. Transcend today, I think, is valued around seven billion dollars.
Most of that is off of a business built in Africa. Hisense, the white goods maker, has a big manufacturing operation in South Africa, as do other Chinese companies for the African market. This is one of the very big trends that we’re seeing globally is that the Chinese are pushing their manufacturing out to the global south, not to export back to China or to the rest of the world.
That was always what we thought they were going to have. The offshoring was to export either back to China or to the rest of the world. Instead, it’s for other African markets.
GERAUD NEEMA: But at the same time as well, because that’s been one narrative that people kind of put forward to say Africa can replace European markets, which is not true. No, but that’s ridiculous. Yes, exactly.
This is one of the challenges that when you mention things like that, people think that, yes, China is not looking at Africa as an alternative European market. That’s not the case.
ERIC OLANDER: Just think about it this way. BYD, if they sell a car to a German consumer in Frankfurt, how many cars do they have to sell to Nigerian consumers to make up for the profit of just that one car? So Africa is not going to replace.
Asia is not going to replace. This is why the talks between China and Europe now are so important. But China’s world is getting smaller.
The G7 countries are restricting access. So the global south countries do become more important, like Africa, which is why I think they’re setting up here. We’re getting some trade numbers as well from Du Xiaohui, who is the top diplomat for China in Africa.
The one who was there before Wu Peng, by the way. Again, touting these increase in trade numbers. But the trade numbers, though, are going up.
But part of the reason they’re going up is because there’s more exports coming from China into Africa. Now, unlike other parts of the world where the export surge is a lot of it in consumer goods, a lot of it is in cars here in Africa, a lot of it is in intermediate goods. Healthy exports, in some respects, that is good because intermediate goods are chemicals and machinery and things that help businesses create products.
GERAUD NEEMA: It’s depending on the countries, because when you look at, when you kind of break the numbers, you’re going to realize that, for example, Nigeria, which is China’s second-largest market and the largest market in terms of Chinese exports. One of the big, in the top five, I was really shocked, the top five products that China was exporting to Nigeria was fake hair, wigs.
ERIC OLANDER: You’re like… No, but that’s been a big market for a long time.
GERAUD NEEMA: How do you make wigs being in the top five export in your countries? So depending on the country, in countries like Congo, South Africa, many countries where Zimbabwe, you see a lot of intermediary goods, you see a lot of manufactured goods, equipment and everything, which somehow tells you a story like China is exporting to this country what this country needs to produce to send back to China. When you now look into the smaller countries, that’s not producing a lot.
This is where you see a lot of like everyday goods. Pants and pants. Exactly.
Shoes, plastic shoes. You see any forms of shoes, wigs, a lot of them. But when you see other countries, the big countries, you’re going to realize there is a pattern where you realize now that those who are even buying from China are, and lots of them being Chinese companies based in these
countries, are now importing from China the equipment they do need for the mining activities in the DRC, in Zambia, in Zimbabwe, in South Africa and all of that.
South Africa, of course, is different. South Africa is the only one that has a kind of basket balance that’s kind of healthy. You have a half manufactured goods, half consumer goods in terms of export, you see.
But export is different, because export is more of natural resources more than anything else.
ERIC OLANDER: But still big trade deficits. Yes. And people flame me on YouTube and X for continuing to bring up this question of the trade deficits.
It’s not me. It’s South Africans who are unhappy with the trade deficit with China.
ERIC OLANDER: Cyril Ramaphosa himself has brought this issue up in his engagements, that South Africans feel exposed and vulnerable when they are that, there’s such a big imbalance in trade. So is resolving that, do you think going to be a priority? Or is it just now offsetting the US and diversifying trade?
COBUS VAN STADEN: I think at the moment, it’s kind of, it’s damage control, right, kind of, because they’re having the US moving on them, you know, so they have to, they have to do something, you know, kind of to offset that. But I think in the longer term, they are interested in, you know, in rebalancing that trade and locating more, you know, kind of more processing and all of this on, you know, in South Africa. And South Africa can do a lot of that, because it has more of an industrial ecosystem.
GERAUD NEEMA: But you guys are talking about rebalancing trade, you’re taking that from South African perspective, as I said here, South Africa and China have two different narratives about the trade. So when Sierra Leone is complaining about the trade deficits of Africa, when Wupang drops those numbers, no officials come and say, by the way, those are the numbers, those are not the numbers of our trades. This is the problem that we have in that narrative.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Gero, just to be clear, does the difference come from China counting exports that are going out of South African ports? Or like, why is there that difference?
GERAUD NEEMA: When I opened, when I dig deep in the situation, I realized that, for example, one of the main elements that drives the number of that offset number from China is like gold and the gold coming from South Africa. Somehow you look at the numbers of other countries, the DRC, the Zambia and everything, export to South Africa, you don’t see gold. But somehow gold in South Africa is the top main element that goes to China, that China counts as coming from South Africa.
So where that gold is coming from, we don’t know. But for South Africa is that. You go to South African Revenue Service, you look at a number, the numbers are different.
The products are kind of different. So when you have that narrative like trade deficit, I’m like, why South Africa never call out Chinese officials and say, by the way, the numbers are not the same.
ERIC OLANDER: So for a long time, for many, many years, South Africa has been the largest trade partner for China in Africa, accounting for about a third. But there’s been a question about how much of that is actually South African products. A lot of materials come from the DRC, go down to the Port of Durban and get classified as a South African export, even though they are mineral products from other countries.
So I thought that South African products have filtered their way through. And so that’s one of the reasons why the number for South Africa has been so high.
GERAUD NEEMA: I thought that was the case until you opened the numbers of China. You realize that, as I mentioned, gold, DRC doesn’t export gold to South Africa. Zambia does not. Zimbabwe does not
GERAUD NEEMA: They do. But when you look at the top 10, cobalt is not even the top 10 of what China counts as coming from South Africa. So you realize that, no, China is counting something else being the one that’s driving South Africa’s trade surplus.
It’s really not cobalt, it’s not copper. I was expecting to see lithium. No, you have gold, chromium, platinum, all coming from South Africa.
But I mean, South Africa is a big gold producer, right? Exactly. This is the element.
ERIC OLANDER: Let me just understand that you’re saying that the numbers from other countries, the products, are not being counted. Are not reflected. So the number we see is a pure South African number.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Exactly, exactly. But counted differently on the different sides.
GERAUD NEEMA: Counted different on the both sides. Because China has a rule when they release every time there is a new rules of origin. They say clearly, things that are coming from X country, transit to another country’s ports, does not count as that.
They count as country origin, the country where the product was manufactured or was extracted. So this is where I say, in that narrative, at some points of Africans, when Wu Peng says that, they have to tell you, what’s the numbers? What stories are we talking about here?
ERIC OLANDER: He seems like a pretty accessible guy, so you might want to send him an email. I have his email address, so you can go ahead and send him an email and be like, Wu Peng, what are you talking about?
GERAUD NEEMA: Because it’s not the first time, because every time Ducey Ahoy or Wu Peng drop these numbers, you don’t see any South African official ever, never raising the point like, this is not the numbers. But when Khamaposa went to China, they talk about trade deficit and everything. But interesting enough, in the joint communique at the end, China did not mention the fact that.
ERIC OLANDER: Oh, that’s the last thing they wanted, because it feeds right into the Western criticism of overcapacity. But by the way, Khamaposa is not alone. Yoweri Museveni has brought this up many times.
William Ruto has brought it up here in Kenya many times. So this is actually not a Western critique. This is very much an African critique.
They want more access. The point you’ve made many times is that many African countries, 33 African countries, in fact, had duty-free access into the Chinese market long before May. And it really didn’t fundamentally change the dynamics.
GERAUD NEEMA: Even funny, let me drop in something on that. Senegal. Senegal, who for long years, for many years, the main export to Senegal to China was groundnuts.
Groundnuts really, like, you know, groundnuts export to China. Until 2024, they eat oil. They get the free access to, they get the free, the zero tariff to China.
You know what came first? Oil became first. 2025, oil jumped, groundnuts dropped sixth in the list of what Senegal export to China.
So it just tells you that even African countries themselves are like, OK, we want free trade, we want access to China. But at the end, it will always go for the high value product being natural resources.
ERIC OLANDER: Yeah. Interesting on this discrepancy on the trade numbers. We also see this in the debt numbers, that the accounting, and this was the issue in Zambia, is that the accounting of debt by the host, or borrowing, country and the accounting of debt by China oftentimes is very different.
And experts like Deborah Brautigam and Yufan Huang, others who study debt, have long complained that there are multiple sets of books on what the true debt numbers are. Sri Lanka had this problem, how much the Chinese owed the Sri Lankans and how much the Sri Lankans thought they owed the Chinese. Oftentimes we’re not the same.
So this data problem is a very big problem. Another story that happened this week is we got news that the Tazara Railway and the Lobito Corridor, these are two of the big mineral railway corridors in southern Africa, stretching from the Atlantic coast all the way over to the Indian Ocean coast, are going to be linked up.
Now, this has been a long time dream in Africa to have Pan-African railways north to south, east to west. It looks like it might come. Giro, you’ve been following this story for a long time and the different pieces.
Let’s just step back first. The Lobedo Corridor is very much a project of the Biden administration, project of the West, of the Global Gateway. The Europeans, Ivanhoe, the Canadians are involved in it.
And the Tazara Railway is very much involved with the Chinese. The Chinese signed a deal for $1.9 billion to resuscitate and revive the Tazara. Now they want to link them together.
Is this fantasy? Is it reality? Is this someone projecting something that we don’t see?
GERAUD NEEMA: What’s going on? I want to be African here by saying, by starting to correct, because if you say that we’re going to get married, no, Lobito, Benguela and Tazara are fully African first. Benguela was built by the Portuguese.
Benguela was built by the Portuguese. Yeah, but it’s still an African project.
ERIC OLANDER: But the money came, I mean, from the Biden administration and that whole Build Back Better World.
GERAUD NEEMA: If you have to, the context would be the Benguela was refurbished. No, not refurbished, was fully rebuilt by China until 2013. $1.8 billion was put on the table. And after that, now they have the modernization with the construction led by Trafigura, where Chinese company lost the bid against that. And then you have on the other side now, after losing on the other side, you have interest coming from Chinese companies to say, OK, we’re going to also refurbish the Tazara one, where we’re going to put $1.4 billion in that project. But in the middle, you have the DRC and Zambia, because none of these countries kind of, Zambia and Angola and Tanzania are not connected.
So to get to the point that you were mentioning, last week on October 29th, what President of João Lourenço was visiting in Tanzania, they say, you know, they made a declaration that both countries have agreed to connect the Benguela Railway and the Tazara to connect from ocean to ocean, Indian Ocean to Atlantic Ocean. It’s interesting because it’s really going to be something to connect. It’s going to be a dream project.
But two things. First thing, I didn’t see much of an announcement from the country where those railroads are going through, especially for the Tanzania, but the Tazara one, Zambia did not make a statement about that.
ERIC OLANDER: But Tanzania, if I understand correctly, does not have the authority to make a unilateral decision on this, because the Tazara is a joint effort. It’s a joint, Tanzania and Zambia.
ERIC OLANDER: So it has to do everything in conjunction with Zambia.
ERIC OLANDER: So there’s reasons for doubt because there was not a joint declaration from Zambia.
GERAUD NEEMA: Exactly, because the connection will happen on Zambian territory. So and there is a pro, there was a feasibility study that was done to extend the Benguela into Zambia. And that’s going to create a new railway.
It was like five billion dollars that was kind of coming out of feasibility study. So we have to connect that. That’s another element.
But that project itself, if it’s come to, you know, to be materialized, interesting part for me was like the fact that both presidents kind of step away from the old geopolitical narrative around how external media, Western countries talk about Tazara and Benguela to say, you know what, it’s, you know, geopolitics, great power competition. By making that statement, they’re basically telling you it’s not about you. It’s about us.
It’s about us, our agency. It’s us, what we want, what we want to make to happen. Of course, maybe Zambia will come later and make a statement about that.
But it’s basically signaling that if ever any of you outside ever think that the Tazara and Benguela are going to be used for a geopolitical narrative, it doesn’t need to work. It’s about us. We want to connect our continent, want to make that happen.
So now that becomes another question, which one is going to be more profitable and which one is going to gain more. But that’s another debate. But the reality is, in terms of narrative, it’s communicating the idea that it’s first about Africa development, integration, and it’s African story.
COBUS VAN STADEN: Yeah, I mean, you know, it’s historically huge, you know, like, if they can do it, it’ll be amazing.
ERIC OLANDER: But again, it changes the dynamic of these railways, because right now, these railways feel like they’re, you know, mined to port, which is a very colonial art construction. So by making it a pan African, it can start actually to fulfill other objectives beyond just bringing raw materials out to the port. I don’t think it will change much, though.
I don’t think it has the potential, though. It has the potential. OK, so you could be bringing raw materials out to the ports and then you could be bringing in parts and other things and toys and whatever.
And commerce just starts to happen. And remember, the biggest problem of the AFCFTA, that’s the African Continental Free Trade Area, is logistics and moving stuff from point A to point B in Africa. This could be part of that solution.
GERAUD NEEMA: For me, when I think of the connection, I think of from the Angolan perspective of like, what’s going to happen to the port of Lobito in Angola? Why? Because Africa trade in Southern Africa is heavily, heavily East leaning.
So all the ports along the eastern Indian Ocean, Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Lamu, all these ports are the main drivers. So when you connect that with Lobito, if you’re in Angola, the question can become, OK, what’s the gain?
ERIC OLANDER: Right. Well, you could it might be cheaper, actually, to put stuff on rail. Yeah.
Take it to Dar es Salaam than it is to actually send things around the Cape of Good Hope.
ERIC OLANDER: So it could completely undermine the whole Lobito railway corridor project. Exactly.
GERAUD NEEMA: That has always been my hypothesis. And for me, it’s the only thing that can make now the Lobito and the Benguela to be relevant to the rest of the continent. If we now open a big trade from Latin America, coming from Brazil, coming from this continent there, having product that countries in Eastern Africa would need, that will be a game changer.
